Use the same analysis rows

Fit the same 150 store-level baseline profiles as Lesson 4. Design columns are [1, lead, urban, demand−100, promotion_share, lead×urban]. There are no treatment indicators because the baseline precedes all alert policies.

Case seed: 20261109. All ten labs use the same store IDs and underlying records. Read the shared data dictionary.

Reproduce the calculation

Run the same fits, covariance calculations, pointwise bands, contrasts, joint tests, and nested comparisons used in the main lesson. The added code also verifies the omitted-variable identity and unchanged predictions after centering.

s = world()['stores']
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(s)),s.lead_days,s.urban,s.baseline_demand-100,s.promotion_share,s.lead_days*s.urban])
beta = np.linalg.lstsq(X, s.baseline_rate, rcond=None)[0]
rural_slope = beta[1]
urban_slope = beta[1] + beta[5]
assert np.isclose(urban_slope, lesson_result(5)['urban_slope'])

# Fit the same baseline stores; HC1 is the course robust covariance.
from scipy.stats import norm, t, f as f_dist, chi2
stores = world()['stores']
x = stores.lead_days.to_numpy(); y = stores.baseline_rate.to_numpy()
u = stores.urban.to_numpy(); demand = stores.baseline_demand.to_numpy()-100
promo = stores.promotion_share.to_numpy(); n = len(y)
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n),x,u,demand,promo,x*u])
b, V, residual = fit_ols(X,y); fitted = X@b
p = X.shape[1]; B = np.linalg.inv(X.T@X)
sigma2_full = residual@residual/(n-p)
classical_se = np.sqrt(np.diag(sigma2_full*B))
robust_se = np.sqrt(np.diag(V)); z_score = b/robust_se
p_value = 2*norm.sf(np.abs(z_score))
ci95 = np.column_stack([b-1.96*robust_se,b+1.96*robust_se])
ci99 = np.column_stack([b-norm.ppf(.995)*robust_se,b+norm.ppf(.995)*robust_se])
# Simple-model pointwise bands use a classical future-variance model.
S = np.column_stack([np.ones(n),x]); bs, Vs, es = fit_ols(S,y)
s2 = es@es/(n-2); bread = np.linalg.inv(S.T@S)
grid = np.linspace(2,5,101); G = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(grid)),grid])
mean = G@bs; mean_se = np.sqrt(s2*np.einsum('ij,jk,ik->i',G,bread,G))
prediction_se = np.sqrt(s2+mean_se**2); critical = t.ppf(.975,n-2)
mean_band = np.column_stack([mean-critical*mean_se,mean+critical*mean_se])
prediction_band = np.column_stack([mean-critical*prediction_se,mean+critical*prediction_se])
row4 = np.array([1,4]); mean4 = row4@bs
mean_se4 = np.sqrt(s2*(row4@bread@row4)); prediction_se4 = np.sqrt(s2+mean_se4**2)
# Recover the omitted-variable identity without changing the sample.
L = np.column_stack([np.ones(n),x,u]); bl, Vl, el = fit_ols(L,y)
sorting, _, _ = fit_ols(S,u); ovb_product = bl[2]*sorting[1]
assert np.isclose(bs[1],bl[1]+ovb_product)
# Centering delivery changes the reference, not fitted values.
C = np.column_stack([np.ones(n),x-3,u,demand,promo,(x-3)*u])
bc, Vc, ec = fit_ols(C,y)
assert np.allclose(C@bc,fitted)
contrasts = []
for lead in [2,3,4,5]:
    c = np.array([0,0,1,0,0,lead]); value = c@b; se = np.sqrt(c@V@c)
    contrasts.append([lead,value,se,value-1.96*se,value+1.96*se])
urban_slope_row = np.array([0,1,0,0,0,1])
urban_slope_se = np.sqrt(urban_slope_row@V@urban_slope_row)
# A two-restriction test asks whether the group lines coincide.
R = np.eye(p)[[2,5]]; restrictions = R@b; RV = R@V@R.T
wald = restrictions@np.linalg.solve(RV,restrictions); wald_p = chi2.sf(wald,2)
A = np.column_stack([np.ones(n),x,demand,promo]); ba, Va, ea = fit_ols(A,y)
F = ((ea@ea-residual@residual)/2)/(residual@residual/(n-p))
F_p = f_dist.sf(F,2,n-p)
# Add centered curvature on the same rows and inspect nested training fit.
Q = np.column_stack([X,(demand/10)**2]); bq,Vq,eq = fit_ols(Q,y)
P = X[:,:5]; bp,Vp,ep = fit_ols(P,y)
sst = np.sum((y-y.mean())**2); fit_rows = []
for label,design,error in [('Lead only',S,es),('Add urban',L,el),('Add demand / promo',P,ep),('Group slopes',X,residual),('Add demand squared',Q,eq)]:
    count = design.shape[1]; sse = error@error
    fit_rows.append([label,count,1-sse/sst,1-(sse/(n-count))/(sst/(n-1)),np.sqrt(sse/n)])
def vif_values(design):
    values = []
    for j in range(1,design.shape[1]):
        other = np.delete(design,j,axis=1); target = design[:,j]
        error = target-other@np.linalg.lstsq(other,target,rcond=None)[0]
        values.append(np.sum((target-target.mean())**2)/(error@error))
    return np.array(values)
raw_vif = vif_values(X); centered_vif = vif_values(C)
# Predictions keep the full profile visible.
profiles = []
for group in [0,1]:
    for lead in [2,3,4,5]:
        row = np.array([1,lead,group,0,.25,lead*group])
        profiles.append([group,lead,row@b])
assert np.all(prediction_band[:,1]-prediction_band[:,0] > mean_band[:,1]-mean_band[:,0])
assert np.allclose(b[[1,5]],[1.53089239224744,.22833509751825537])
assert np.isclose(bc[2],contrasts[1][1])
assert np.allclose(X.T@residual,0,atol=1e-8)

The code runs after the shared setup in the notebook. The downloadable script includes that setup and runs on its own.

Read the model and uncertainty

The displayed RMSE is in-sample fit on store-average baseline rates. Changing the input set changes the comparison; it does not by itself identify the causal effect of altering delivery time.

Change one analytical choice

Change the reference delivery time and verify that fitted values stay fixed. Then change one profile contrast and recalculate its variance from the full covariance matrix. Compare a joint restriction with an individual restriction.

Reconstruct uncertainty and adjusted comparisons

A covariance matrix connects every coefficient to its uncertainty

b = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy; classical Var(b) = s²(XᵀX)⁻¹

X contains an intercept and all transformed input columns. Its full column rank identifies unique coefficients. Use a least-squares solver rather than a matrix inverse for estimation. Here p is the number of columns including the intercept, and s²=SSE/(n−p).

Classical slope precision depends on residual spread and predictor spread

SE(slope)=s/√Sxx; SE(intercept)=s√[1/n+X̄²/Sxx]

For simple OLS, Sxx=Σ(X−X̄)² and s²=SSE/(n−2). Under independent normal constant-variance errors, coefficient statistics follow Student t with n−2 degrees of freedom. An intercept at a distant zero can be imprecise even when mean predictions near X̄ are precise.

HC1 and HC3 change uncertainty while preserving the OLS fit

HC1 = [n/(n−p)] B Xᵀdiag(e²)XB; B=(XᵀX)⁻¹

HC3 replaces each eᵢ² by eᵢ²/(1−hᵢ)² without the HC1 prefactor; hᵢ=xᵢᵀBxᵢ. Both preserve OLS coefficients and allow heteroskedasticity across independent rows. The displayed robust intervals use HC1 and a normal reference; the classical band uses a t reference and constant future variance.

A future individual adds residual variance to mean-estimation variance

Var(mean at x₀)=x₀ᵀVar(b)x₀; classical prediction variance=s²+x₀ᵀs²Bx₀

The added s² represents a new independent outcome’s variance. For simple regression this becomes s²[1+1/n+(x₀−X̄)²/Sxx]. A robust covariance estimate for b does not automatically determine that new outcome’s conditional variance. The plotted bands are pointwise, and target the same eight-week store-average measurement.

Profile uncertainty includes covariance between coefficients

Estimate=cᵀb; SE=√(cᵀVc)

For an urban-minus-nonurban comparison at lead L, c=[0,0,1,0,0,L]. Thus variance=Vurban,urban+L²Vinteraction,interaction+2L Vurban,interaction. For the urban lead slope, c=[0,1,0,0,0,1]. Using the covariance terms is essential when adding coefficients.

A joint restriction uses the covariance of the whole restricted vector

W = (Rb−r)ᵀ(RVRᵀ)⁻¹(Rb−r) → χ²(q)

R selects the tested linear combinations and r states their null values. Here R selects urban and lead×urban, r is zero, and q=2. HC1 supplies V. This asymptotic robust Wald test differs from the exact classical F test under normal constant-variance errors.

The classical F test compares nested residual sums of squares

F = [(SSE restricted−SSE full)/q] / [SSE full/(n−p)]

The restricted model omits both location terms but retains lead, demand, and promotions. On the same 150 observations, F=59.349 with (2,144) degrees of freedom and p=1.59e-19. Its constant-variance justification is separate from the HC1 Wald result.

Centering preserves fitted values while changing the reference comparison

Reparameterizing these interaction columns
TermVIF before centeringVIF after lead−3
Urban11.851.29
Lead×urban12.372.23

For each non-intercept column, regress it on all other columns and compute VIF=1/(1−R²). Centering can reduce reference-related overlap in an interaction basis, but does not create new information or fix fundamentally redundant predictors. Fitted values, residuals, and equivalent contrasts remain unchanged.

Shared control slopes distinguish this model from unrestricted group fits

Current model: group-specific intercept and lead slope; shared demand and promotion slopes

Separate unrestricted group fits would also allow the demand and promotion coefficients to differ. They match a pooled model only when the corresponding group interactions are included. As an optional extension, add centered-demand×promotion and interpret its demand slope at two promotion shares; keep the main terms and evaluate the resulting comparison on the same rows.

How this case is generated

The shared world contains 150 stores followed for 32 weeks. Delivery time, location, demand, promotions, store differences, and a common time pattern generate the probability of a stockout. Each store-week contains 140 product-days. The generator draws their availability and records both policy paths using the same underlying draws.

The expected alert reduction varies with delivery time and location. Offers are randomized only within the 50-store pilot cohort. Voluntary adoption uses measured starting conditions in a separate cohort. The final cohort starts a selected rollout in week 25. These are distinct studies inside the same business history.

Inspect the numerical mechanism

p0 = 0.055 + 0.014 × lead + 0.0005 × (demand − 100) + 0.018 × urban + 0.003 × (lead − 3) × urban + 0.020 × promotion + store effect + 0.006 × sin(week / 4)

Expected reduction = 0.006 + 0.008 × lead + 0.004 × urban; p1 = p0 − reduction

The probabilities are converted to counts by comparing 140 uniform draws with p0 or p1. Cost is 6 CU per stockout product-day plus 20 CU per week when alerts are offered. These costs are the stated management accounting scenario. The complete assignment rules, random streams, and calculations are in the shared source.

Read the shared generator and analysis source

Compare with the known answer

The baseline mechanism includes a delivery-by-location interaction. Its known presence does not guarantee that a particular sample yields a statistically significant estimate. Compare the estimate and interval with the mechanism only after interpreting the observed data.
